passage:
Amma pulled a crumpled paper from the bottom of Jahnavi's bag. "Science test. Nineteen out of twenty? Why is this crushed like a peanut wrapper?"
Jahnavi, ten, kept her eyes on her rice. "No reason."
"Last month you stuck your prize certificate on the fridge."
"I took it down."
"I noticed. Why?"
A long pause. "Rafiq and them call me Show-off Jahnavi now. Every time Ma'am reads the marks, they go 'ooooh' and clap slowly."
"So you hide your papers."
"If nobody sees, they forget. Yesterday I said I got twelve. They let me sit with them."
Amma sat down beside her. "And how did twelve feel?"
Jahnavi shrugged, and her eyes filled.

qa.q: What mark did Jahnavi get in the science test?
qa.a: Nineteen out of twenty.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi want when claiming to have got twelve?
qa.a: Jahnavi wanted to be accepted again and sit with the group without being called a show-off.

qa.q: Amma's question "And how did twelve feel?" opens a door. What could Amma do next?
qa.a: Amma could listen to how hurt and lonely Jahnavi feels, and then speak with the class teacher about the slow clapping, rather than just telling Jahnavi to be proud.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see the "ooooh" and the slow clapping?
qa.a: Rafiq may think it is just a joke and not see how much it hurts, or may feel a little envious of Jahnavi's marks.

grounding: A girl who won a prize hides her good marks after classmates mock her as a show-off.

passage: I'm Kamal, and in Class 6 I won the district maths prize. The headmaster read my name at assembly, and I felt tall for about one morning. By lunch, the kids at my table were saying, "Oh, Professor Kamal, please solve my tiffin," and bowing. Someone wrote SHOW-OFF on my desk in chalk. So I changed. When tests came back, I folded mine face down. When Sir asked who got full marks, I kept my hand in my lap. Only Rukmini noticed. "You used to be proud," she said. I told her I didn't care about marks. That wasn't true. I just cared more about lunch.

qa.q: What was written on Kamal's desk in chalk?
qa.a: SHOW-OFF.

qa.q: What does "I just cared more about lunch" reveal about Kamal's feelings?
qa.a: It shows Kamal still valued the marks but feared being left out at lunch even more.

qa.q: Rukmini's comment was a chance to open up. What could Kamal have done then?
qa.a: Kamal could have admitted the teasing hurt and asked Rukmini, or a teacher, for help, instead of pretending not to care.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel watching Kamal fold tests face down?
qa.a: Rukmini seems to miss how proud Kamal used to be, and may feel sad that the teasing made Kamal hide. 😔

grounding: A child who won a maths prize is mocked as a show-off and starts hiding test results to fit in.

passage: Note for the file and for the parents of Shankar (Class 5). Since Shankar won the school essay prize last month, I have noticed a change. Classmates started calling him 'show-off' and 'teacher's pet', mostly at recess. This week his essay was half a page, flat, with spelling mistakes in words he spelled correctly in September. When I returned it, he looked relieved at the low grade and showed it to the boys at his table. I spoke to him privately. He said, 'If I'm bad, they'll stop.' Plan: talk to the class about teasing without naming him, praise effort for everyone rather than only toppers, and meet his parents on Friday. — Lokesh Iyer, class teacher

qa.q: Which prize did Shankar win last month?
qa.a: The school essay prize.

qa.q: Why did Shankar look relieved at the low grade?
qa.a: Shankar hoped a poor grade would stop the teasing, believing that being bad would make the others stop.

qa.q: Which part of Lokesh Iyer's plan might help Shankar most, and why?
qa.a: Praising effort for everyone, not only toppers, could make doing well feel less like standing apart, so classmates stop treating Shankar as a target.

qa.q: How might Shankar's parents feel on reading this note?
qa.a: They may be surprised and worried that their child is hiding real ability, and grateful the teacher noticed early.

grounding: A teacher notices a prize-winning boy deliberately writing badly after classmates mock him as a show-off.

passage:
Friday

Today Ma'am gave back the Hindi test. I got 48 out of 50. Pradeep leaned over to see and I turned it face down fast. He asked, and I said 35. He said, "Good, you're human."
Ever since I won the spelling trophy at assembly, the boys in my row call me Show-off Sid. They bow when I walk past. Pradeep does it too, and he used to share his chips with me.
So now I don't put up my hand even when I know. In maths I knew the answer was 72 and I just sat there. It was a weird feeling, like holding in a sneeze.
Mummy wants to frame the trophy certificate and keeps calling me her clever boy. I told her to keep it in the cupboard.
Sid

qa.q: What mark did Sid actually get in the Hindi test?
qa.a: He got 48 out of 50.

qa.q: How does Sid feel about hiding his answers now?
qa.a: It feels uncomfortable and wrong to him, "like holding in a sneeze", but he does it to stop the teasing.

qa.q: How could a teacher or Mummy support Sid without making the teasing worse?
qa.a: They could praise him privately, keep his results quiet in class, and talk with the class about cheering for each other.

qa.q: What might Pradeep be feeling when he says "Good, you're human"?
qa.a: Pradeep may feel relieved that Sid seems ordinary again, perhaps because the prize made him feel left behind.

grounding: A child mocked as a show-off after winning a prize starts hiding his good marks to fit in.

passage: Yamini found the test paper under the straw in the goat shed, folded into a tight square. Mathematics, 50 out of 50, a star in red ink. She held it up when her brother Ramesh came in with the fodder. "Why is this with the goats?" Ramesh, eleven, grabbed it. "Give it." "You came first in the whole taluka last month. Why hide a test?" He stared at the goat. "On the school bus they call me Collector Saheb. They salute and say 'Show-off, show-off' till we reach the bridge. Yesterday Balu said I think I'm better than the village." "Do you?" "No! I just like numbers." He pushed the paper into his pocket. "If I get sixties now, they'll forget."

qa.q: Where did Yamini find the test paper?
qa.a: She found it under the straw in the goat shed, folded into a tight square.

qa.q: Why does Ramesh want to hide his full marks?
qa.a: He is hurt by the teasing on the bus and hopes that if his marks look ordinary, the others will forget and accept him again.

qa.q: What could Yamini do next to help her brother?
qa.a: She could tell their parents or his teacher about the bus teasing and remind Ramesh that liking numbers is nothing to hide.

qa.q: How might Balu see Ramesh's taluka prize?
qa.a: Balu may feel that Ramesh's win makes the other village children look smaller, so mocking him feels like evening things out.

grounding: A child mocked as a show-off after winning a prize begins hiding his marks to fit in again.

passage:
Thursday
Today at assembly I got the Best Student prize. Everyone clapped. I was so happy I couldn't stop smiling.
Then at lunch Keerthana said, "Here comes Miss Show-off," and the whole table laughed. When I sat down, two girls moved their tiffins away.
In the afternoon, the maths test came back. I got 19 out of 20. Keerthana asked, "How much?" and I said, "Not much, 12 only." I don't know why I lied. I just wanted them to laugh with me again, not at me.
I hid the prize certificate in my bag instead of showing Abbu at the gate.
Zeenat

qa.q: What mark did Zeenat really get in the maths test?
qa.a: Zeenat got 19 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat say "12 only" instead of the real mark?
qa.a: Zeenat felt hurt and left out after being called a show-off, and hoped hiding the good mark would win the group back.

qa.q: How could a teacher or Abbu support Zeenat?
qa.a: They could celebrate the prize warmly, talk with Zeenat about the teasing, and help the class learn to be happy for each other.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel on learning that Zeenat was hiding the prize?
qa.a: Keerthana might feel surprised or a little guilty, not realising how much the joke hurt.

grounding: A child who wins a school prize is mocked as a show-off and starts hiding good marks to fit in.

passage:
Chaitanya won first prize in the district quiz and came back to the village school with a steel trophy. The headmaster made him stand on the verandah while everyone clapped.
But on the walk home past the fields, Lavanya and three other children kept calling, "Oh, the big quiz king! Too good for us now?" One of them pretended to bow.
The next week, when the half-yearly results came, Chaitanya folded his report card small and put it inside his math book. When someone asked his marks, he said, "Just average." He stopped raising his hand in class.
At home he put the trophy behind the grain tin, where nobody would see it.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya put the trophy at home?
qa.a: He put the trophy behind the grain tin.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya start saying his marks were "just average"?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt by the teasing, and wanted to fit in again instead of standing out.

qa.q: What could the headmaster or his parents do to help Chaitanya?
qa.a: They could praise his effort privately, notice the teasing and talk to the class about cheering each other's success.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see the teasing?
qa.a: Lavanya might think it is just fun, not realising it made Chaitanya hide his success and stop raising his hand.

grounding: A child who wins a district quiz is mocked as showing off and starts hiding his marks and trophy to fit in.

passage:
Tariq won the spelling bee at his primary school in Manchester. His name went up on the board in gold letters. He grinned all the way through lunch.
By afternoon, though, Mina and her friends were whispering, "Tariq the genius. Tariq the show-off." When he got 20 out of 20 in the spelling test on Friday, someone groaned loudly, "Of course he did."
The next week Tariq made two mistakes on purpose. When his teacher asked why, he shrugged.
At home, his mum asked about the trophy. "Can we not put it on the shelf?" he said. "I don't want anyone to see it."
He went up to his room and closed the door.

qa.q: What did Tariq win at his school?
qa.a: Tariq won the spelling bee.

qa.q: Why did Tariq make two mistakes on purpose?
qa.a: He felt hurt and embarrassed by being called a show-off, and wanted to seem ordinary so the others would stop teasing.

qa.q: How could Tariq's teacher support him?
qa.a: The teacher could talk to Tariq privately about the teasing and help the class learn to celebrate each other instead of mocking.

qa.q: How might Mina see the change in Tariq?
qa.a: Mina might not notice at all, or might feel pleased he seems less of a show-off, without realising he is hiding his ability.

grounding: A child who wins the spelling bee is mocked as a show-off and starts making mistakes on purpose to fit in.

passage:
The morning after Mridul won the school science prize, a paper sign was stuck on his desk: MR SHOW-OFF. Sahil and two others snickered from the back bench. At lunch, when Mridul explained a sum to a friend, Sahil said loudly, "Oh, here comes the professor." Everyone laughed.
That week, when the maths tests came back, Mridul folded his paper in half before anyone could see the 19 out of 20. When Miss asked who got full marks in the next quiz, he kept his hand down, though he had. On Friday he asked his mother if he could skip the prize photo for the school magazine. She asked why, listened to all of it, and phoned his class teacher that evening.

qa.a: MR SHOW-OFF.

qa.q: Why did Mridul fold his test paper in half?

qa.q: How could Mridul's class teacher help after his mother's call?

qa.q: How might Sahil see his jokes?

passage:

Wednesday: "Spell SHOW-OFF," Mridul said when Vaibhav walked in, and half the class laughed. At lunch nobody saved him a seat. When Miss praised his essay, someone groaned, "Obviously." Vaibhav stared at his tiffin.

passage:
Jasleen, you're sad because the girls called you a show-off after the prize? Come, sit with your Rekha nani. When I was ten, in Amritsar, I won the district essay prize. The next day my friends sang "Rekha big-shot, Rekha big-shot" all through recess. I cried behind the water tank.
After that I started making small mistakes on purpose in my copybook, so my marks wouldn't stand out. For a whole year. Then my mother found my copy full of crossings-out, and I told her everything. That same evening she walked with me to my teacher's house and spoke to her. On the way home she said, "Your gift is not a crime." Slowly I stopped hiding.
Now, show me your certificate.

qa.q: Which prize did young Rekha win?
qa.a: The district essay prize.

qa.q: How did young Rekha feel after the teasing?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, crying behind the water tank and then hiding her ability.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Rekha stop hiding?
qa.a: Telling her mother, who that same evening spoke to the teacher and told her, "Your gift is not a crime."

qa.q: What might Rekha's mother have felt seeing the copybook full of crossings-out?
qa.a: She likely felt worried and sad, then protective once she learned why.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being mocked as a show-off after a prize and hiding her marks to fit in, until her mother stepped in the same day she was told.

passage: On the last day before the summer holidays the school bus was an oven, and Sumit was holding the silver cup for first place in Class 6. It had been announced at assembly. 'Oho, show-off is coming,' Jagdish called from the back seat. Others joined in: 'Sir, sir, I know everything, sir!' Sumit laughed along, but he put the cup in his bag. The bus broke down near the flyover, and they all waited forty minutes on the hot pavement. Nobody sat near him. When the relief bus came, Sumit took out his report card and folded it so the 98 in maths didn't show. At home, when Mummy asked about marks, he said, 'Okay-okay.' That night she found the cup under his bed.

qa.q: Where did the bus break down?
qa.a: Near the flyover.

qa.q: Why did Sumit fold his report card so the 98 didn't show?
qa.a: Sumit felt embarrassed and lonely after being called a show-off, and wanted to fit back in.

qa.q: How could Mummy respond after finding the cup under his bed?
qa.a: She could gently ask what happened, tell him she is proud, and let his class teacher know about the teasing so he doesn't feel he must hide his work.

qa.q: What might Jagdish be feeling when he starts the teasing?
qa.a: Jagdish may feel jealous or left behind, and mocking Sumit might make him feel less small.

passage:
'Oye, Hrithik, where's your gold medal? Wearing it to sleep?' Jagdish blew on his cold hands in the winter-morning line.
'It's at home.'
'Why? Showing off at home also?'
Laughter.
'I didn't even ask for it.'
'Mr Topper didn't ask for it,' Jagdish mimicked. 'Poor Mr Topper.'
In class, Ma'am held up the unit test papers. 'Hrithik, full marks again. Come and—'
'Ma'am, can you just put it on my desk?'
'Don't you want to—'
'No, Ma'am. Please.'
She paused, then placed it face down. Hrithik slid it into his bag without looking.
Jagdish leaned over. 'What happened, topper? Shy now?'
Hrithik shrugged. 'Just got lucky.'

qa.q: Where did Hrithik say the medal was?
qa.a: At home.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik ask Ma'am to put the paper on his desk?
qa.a: Hrithik felt embarrassed and wary, not wanting another round of teasing from Jagdish.

qa.q: What could Ma'am do after noticing Hrithik's request?
qa.a: She could talk to Hrithik privately about the teasing and deal with the mocking in class, so students don't feel they must hide success.

qa.q: What would change if the class cheered Hrithik's full marks instead of mocking?
qa.a: Hrithik would likely feel proud and relaxed, and wouldn't need to claim he 'just got lucky'.

passage: At the Christmas prize day, the principal called my name: "Shankar, first in Class 5!" I walked up so proud, holding the shiny book. But back in class, Disha said, "Oh, look, the show-off." Others laughed. At break, someone copied my walk, chin up in the air. I felt my face go hot. I hadn't even been showing off. The next test, I got full marks. When the teacher handed it back, I quickly folded it so nobody could see. When Disha asked my marks, I said, "Okay-okay." I started hiding my good marks every time. I just wanted them to stop. Mummy found a folded paper in my bag and asked why I didn't show her. I didn't know how to explain.
